t.azul@-36.8,-59.9:
Azul is a quiet city of fifty-four thousand on the open pampas of Buenos Aires province, about three hundred kilometres south-west of the capital, and it begins with a fort. In 1832 a frontier outpost was built on the banks of the Arroyo Azul, the Blue Stream, to guard settlers against raids and to push the line of European settlement farther into the plains. The town grew around it, and the grid of streets, wide plazas and low houses still has a frontier feel.

The land here is almost perfectly flat, a green and gold sea of grass, wheat and cattle pasture, with the sky taking up most of the view. To the north-east rise the low, worn granite hills of the Tandilia system, among the oldest rocks in South America, though a rider coming from the city would hardly call them mountains. The wind is a constant, and it can blow hard enough to lean a motorcycle sideways on the long straights.

As a fuel stop, Azul is perfectly placed. Stations stand along the main road, with convenience stores and often a grill restaurant, and the long distances between towns in this part of Argentina make it wise to fill up when you can. Further south and west, toward the hills of Tornquist and Sierra de la Ventana, the services thin out and stations are farther apart.

Food is the other attraction. Argentine roadside restaurants serve grilled beef, empanadas, milanesas and the sweet pastries called facturas, with strong coffee. A parrilla in the town centre is a good place for a long, unhurried lunch. The portions are large, and the bread is excellent.

The best time to ride this part of the pampas is spring or autumn, when the temperature is mild and the light is soft. Summer can be very hot, with sudden thunderstorms, and winter brings frost and fog on early mornings. A long day across the plains has its own satisfactions, and the sunsets are huge.
t.gwadar@25.1,62.3:
Gwadar sits on a small hammer-shaped peninsula jutting into the Arabian Sea, at the far western end of Pakistan's coast, and for most of its history it belonged to somebody else. The Sultan of Oman held it for nearly two centuries, after receiving it as a gift in the 1780s, and it was only in 1958 that Pakistan bought it back. A few years later a deep-water port began to be developed here, and in recent times Chinese investment has built a large modern port and plans for a city, giving the place a curious mixture of fishing village and building site.

The old town is a small, hot cluster of low buildings and fishing boats on the isthmus, with a long beach on each side of the narrow neck of land. On the east side, the water is shallow and sheltered, and on the west the Arabian Sea rolls in. A rocky headland, Koh-e-Batil, rises at the end of the peninsula, and from its top you see the whole bay and the lines of boats in the harbour. The sunsets are rich, orange and dusty, and fishermen mend their nets on the sand. There are about fifty thousand people in the town.

The ride that ends here is a long one. The Makran Coastal Highway, running from Karachi, passes through Hingol National Park, where wind and water have carved formations that look like a sphinx and a princess, and crosses long stretches of empty desert. The road is a good surface for most of the way, with sea views and almost no traffic, and the heat is fierce in summer. Sandstorms and strong winds can arise suddenly, and the road is long and empty, so it pays to be self-sufficient.

Gwadar has fuel, markets, restaurants serving fresh fish and basic accommodation, and it is the only substantial town for a long way. Fill the tank and your water containers here before heading on, and take care to keep to roads you know. As elsewhere in Balochistan, you may meet security checkpoints, so carry identification and check the current situation before you travel.

Go in the cooler months, from about November to March. The sea breeze at dusk is the reward for a long day in the saddle.
t.ormara@25.2,64.6:
Ormara is a fishing town on a rocky headland that pokes out into the Arabian Sea, and it feels like a place the twentieth century half forgot. About thirteen thousand people live here, in low concrete houses and boat sheds strung along a sheltered bay. A navy base occupies part of the peninsula, but the heart of the town is the harbour, where wooden dhows come in with the catch and the smell of drying fish hangs in the air. A walk to the end of the jetty at dawn, with the boats unloading and gulls wheeling, is as good a morning as the road offers.

The place has a very old story. The Makran coast was the route Alexander the Great's admiral Nearchus took in the fourth century BC when he led the fleet home from the Indus, and ancient writers describe the fish-eating peoples of the shore. Fish are still the staple. The harbour town traded with Oman and the Gulf for centuries, and old links with Arab and East African sailors show in the faces and the dialects along the coast.

To get here, the Makran Coastal Highway runs west from Karachi, over the Hingol River and the Buzi Pass, then drops to the coastal flats. The last stretch into Ormara is quiet, flat and straight, with salt pans and scrub on one side and the sea on the other. The road is generally in good condition, but crosswinds and sand across the surface are common, and distances are big. Speed is not the point; steady cruising and plenty of water are.

Fuel is available in Ormara, which is a proper town with garages, small shops and tea houses, though supplies of petrol can be irregular in this remote part of Balochistan, so fill whenever you can. Simple guesthouses exist, and fresh grilled fish is usually the best thing to order. Heat is the main hazard, and the sensible season is winter, when the air is mild and the sea clear. Summer brings strong monsoon winds and heavy swell.

Ormara's peninsula also has a bird and turtle life that deserves respect. Green turtles and olive ridleys nest on beaches in this stretch of coast, and the headland is a landmark for migrating birds. Check the security advice for Balochistan before you travel, and keep the day's riding within daylight hours.
t.transpantaneira point 2@-16.4,-56.7:
A short way past Poconé the tarmac gives out and the road becomes the Transpantaneira proper. The town is about fifteen kilometres behind, and from here the landscape opens into wet pasture, scattered trees and shining ponds, where herons and ibis wade and cattle graze among them. The track is raised above the flood plain, built on an embankment, and the borrow pits alongside have become permanent lagoons, which is why every ditch seems full of birds.

Fazendas and pousadas along the way offer meals and beds, and some will sell petrol in an emergency, though you should not count on it, and prices will be high. Bring more water than you think necessary, along with sun cream, insect repellent and a hat, since temperatures climb past thirty-five degrees in the dry months.

The riding is slow, sandy and bumpy, and the surface changes with the season. In dry weather it is a corrugated, dusty track where a following vehicle can blind you in a cloud, and sand patches can unsettle a heavy bike. In the wet it can turn to slick mud and ruts, and sections may be impassable. The wooden bridges deserve respect: planks can be loose or missing, and a gap in the deck is a nasty surprise. Cross them slowly, in a straight line, and walk first if you are unsure.

This is also a place to slow your mind. The Pantanal belongs to the cowboys, the pantaneiros, who ride out with the herds and know the rhythm of the water. Their stories and their grilled beef are part of the welcome. Dawn and dusk are the hours when animals are most active and the light is most gentle, so plan your day around them, and be off the road before dark, since cattle and wildlife drift onto it at night and the starlight is no help.
t.transpantaneira point 3@-17.4,-56.8:
Porto Jofre is where the Transpantaneira stops, at a broad bend of the Cuiaba River deep in the Pantanal, and it is a place of a few lodges, a boat ramp and an enormous quantity of sky. There is no town, only a small cluster of buildings serving fishermen, naturalists and the occasional rider, and Poconé is a long way back, more than a hundred kilometres. You come here for a single reason: this stretch of river is one of the best places on Earth to see wild jaguars.

The big cats hunt along the banks, taking caimans, capybaras and fish, and the local boat guides know where to look. Boat trips leave early in the morning and in the afternoon, and sightings are frequent enough that the place has become world-famous among wildlife photographers. Take a trip, even if you are used to seeing animals from a bike seat; seeing a jaguar slide into the water to chase a caiman is not an experience you forget. Book through a lodge in advance in the busy season.

Fuel is a question to settle before you arrive. Meals and rooms are simple and fairly costly, because everything has to come down the dirt road. Mosquitoes can be fierce at dusk, so long sleeves are a better idea than clever sprays.

The river is a lifeline here, and the wet season changes everything. When the water rises, the plain becomes a lake with cattle on islands, and boat traffic replaces the road. In the dry season the river runs lower and the animals concentrate along its banks, making it the better time for spotting. At night the sky is clear and dark, with frogs singing and a smell of mud and water plants. The ride back is the same long dusty road, so give yourself a full day and leave at first light.
